topic: Thread Oversubscription: The Dynamic Difficulty of Manual Tuning
explanation: Assumption: A fixed ratio of software threads to hardware threads can be determined for optimal performance. Reality: Manually managing raw threads often leads to oversubscription (too many runnable threads), which degrades performance due to excessive context switching and poor cache utilization. Why It Fails: The optimal ratio is highly dynamic, depending on whether the program is currently I/O-heavy or computation-heavy. Furthermore, performance tuning is dependent on specific machine architecture (cache details, core count), meaning a solution tuned for one platform is unlikely to work well or avoid oversubscription on others.
code_example: /* Manual management requires complex logic to balance load against available cores, often using hardware_concurrency() as a starting point, but failing to adapt dynamically. */
practical_example: A developer sets up a thread pool size based on `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()`. When the program enters an I/O wait state, most threads become blocked. When it returns to a computation state, the pool may be too large for the suddenly available resources, causing severe context switch overhead.
